Learners on learning forums often state that getting a single test score (such as 7 or 8 out of 10) tells them they passed, but gives them no idea which specific database concepts they actually mastered and which ones need review.
Calculates competency scores across core PostgreSQL concepts and displays an interactive visual radar chart of strengths and weaknesses.

A common complaint on developer communities is that normalization rules (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) feel too theoretical, and learners struggle to explain why a bad schema design leads to data duplication or update anomalies.
Provides short written conceptual questions evaluated using clear rubrics that explain why an answer is incomplete and how to fix the design.
Learners frequently ask questions about multi-table joins, GROUP BY, and subqueries, finding it frustrating when existing practice sites only say 'Wrong Output' without helpful hints.
Runs queries in an isolated Docker container and checks both the query structure and returned rows to give helpful hints on mistakes.
Discussions show that standard multiple-choice quizzes only show correct or incorrect marks without explaining the underlying concept behind a wrong answer.
Identifies the core concept behind missed questions and provides clear written explanations to help learners understand why an answer was wrong.

A common frustration is that fixed exams give every learner the same question set, so strong learners waste effort on easy items while weaker learners face items far above their level, and neither group gets an accurate ability reading.

Design, build, and deploy the DBCAS web platform to evaluate learner competency across the Core PostgreSQL Knowledge Domain using personalized practice plans across multiple-choice, read-only SQL, and rubric-based essay items.

• Verify that every practice session spreads the plan across the selected concepts as far as the exact selected question count allows and meets that count, with SQL items always drawn from the validated bank. • Ensure automated essay scores match administrator grading on test answers. • Keep SQL sandbox query execution under 2 seconds (with a strict 3.0s statement timeout) while keeping execution environments secure. • Complete all planned features across the 5 development sprints.
Build the system using well-known, reliable open-source tools (React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Docker, and a provider-agnostic LLM API) along with sample datasets created by the team.
Helps learners understand their weaknesses, decide which topics to study first, and gives administrators clear evidence of progress on course learning goals.
Follow the 15-week Capstone 1 schedule from September to late December 2026, meeting all university deadlines: Status Reports 1 to 4, Midterm Demo, Final Report, and Capstone Defense.

Enables administrators to define course learning goals, organize them into the Core PostgreSQL concept model with prerequisite relationships, assign difficulty levels, and review system-suggested mappings.
Administrator: Ensures tight alignment between assessments and university curriculum standards.

Maintains an Administrator-approved, validated library of multiple-choice questions, read-only SQL tasks, and short essay prompts categorized by difficulty, tagged with specific PostgreSQL concepts, tracked through version families, and documented with explanations and source references.
Administrator: Saves time when curating the validated item pool and guarantees balanced topic coverage.

Provides a clean practice interface, with a persistent countdown, 10- and 5-minute warnings, forward-only navigation, autosaved answer drafts, an embedded SQL editor, and English/Vietnamese interface and theme preferences.
Learner: Delivers a smooth, distraction-free environment for answering coding and conceptual questions.

Executes multi-format grading: instant verification for MCQs, isolated Docker execution for read-only SQL queries, and rubric-guided AI scoring for short essays. Every submission waits in an administrator review queue; the administrator checks SQL and essay evidence, adjusts scores if needed, and approves publication.
Learner & Administrator: Eliminates manual grading bottlenecks while delivering consistent results under administrator oversight.

Aggregates evidence across published sessions into radar and bar charts of PostgreSQL competency. After the charts, it shows a “What to study next” list of below-benchmark concepts ordered by shortfall from target, with the concept name and its description when available.
Learner & Administrator: Replaces a single vague score with a transparent breakdown of real abilities.

Compares cumulative published concept scores with the platform's 70% passing target, flags gaps, and provides evidence-linked explanations. The learner's below-benchmark concepts appear after the profile as a ranked “What to study next” list.
Learner: Explains missed concepts and shows which weak topic to study first.

Lets the learner choose the concepts, difficulty bands, question count (1–20, default 5) and source (validated bank or AI) before question one. The system assembles and freezes the complete plan at that moment, spreading it across the selected concepts as far as the exact count allows, with no repeated version families. With source AI, MCQ and essay items may be generated and validated before entering the plan, while SQL items always come from the validated bank; if AI cannot fill the plan, a single bank_mixed notice explains the substitution. A genuine bank shortage stops the start with an explicit explanation rather than a silently shortened session.
Learner: Measures ability with relevant questions and fewer surprises than a fixed exam.

System authenticates users with JWT-based sessions and implements exactly two application roles: User (Learner) and Admin (Administrator). Email/password and OAuth 2.0 (Google, GitHub) sign-in are supported, together with self-service password recovery through a single-use, 15-minute emailed token stored only as a SHA-256 digest. Verified-email OAuth sign-up creates Learner accounts; linking an existing account preserves its roles.
System allows administrators to define course learning outcomes (CLOs), the Core PostgreSQL concept model, difficulty levels, and prerequisite relationships between concepts.
System suggests connections between course outcomes and PostgreSQL concepts using assistive AI, requiring confirmation by the administrator.

System enables administrators to approve AI-generated candidates after automated checks and curate the validated Question Bank: a pool of approved question items spanning multiple-choice, read-only SQL, and short essay formats across the Core PostgreSQL Knowledge Domain, with test data sets, reference answers, explanations, source references, and version lineage.
System analyzes question prompts and recommends relevant concept tags and evaluation criteria for administrator review.

System exposes read-only runtime status (AI evaluator, prompt builder, database and pipeline) and a mandatory two-stage result workflow: AI grading first, then administrator review and approval. Administrators do not choose between automatic and reviewed release. Administrators do not create exams: every learner starts a learner-defined practice session by choosing concepts, difficulty bands (EASY 1–2, MEDIUM 3, HARD 4–5), an exact question count from 1 to 20 (default 5) and a source (validated bank or AI).

System provides learners with a clean practice interface featuring a persistent countdown, 10- and 5-minute remaining warnings, automatic submission at 00:00, a progress indicator, forward-only navigation, autosaved drafts, an embedded SQL code editor, and English/Vietnamese and theme preferences.
System instantly evaluates submitted multiple-choice answers against the verified answer key.

System runs read-only learner SQL (SELECT statements only) inside a secure, isolated PostgreSQL 17 sandbox and grades by semantic and result correctness — executing against multiple test datasets including edge cases and verifying required concept usage when the question mandates a technique — never by exact string matching. DML/DDL knowledge is assessed through MCQ and essay items and is never executed.

System evaluates technical written explanations against administrator rubrics with LLM assistance, providing score breakdowns and constructive feedback. Every submission is reviewed by an administrator, who checks SQL and essay evidence, adjusts scores if needed, and approves publication.

System stores standardized grading evidence for every answer in an organized record capturing the question, question type, PostgreSQL concept, difficulty, learner answer, grading result, and validation information, timestamped per session.

System calculates learner competency levels for each concept deterministically by comparing points earned against total points possible for that concept in a session, and pools point totals across all published sessions for the cumulative profile.
System renders interactive radar and bar charts showing the learner's mastery across core PostgreSQL concepts, including a cumulative view built only from published sessions.

System flags concepts below the expected standard using cumulative published evidence, then presents them after the competency profile as a “What to study next” list ordered by shortfall from target. Each item names the concept and shows its description when available; LLM assistance provides an evidence-linked explanation without changing scores or topic order.

System freezes the selected concepts, difficulty bands, question count and source before question one, then assembles and stores the complete ordered plan, spreads it across the selected concepts as far as the count allows, meets the exact count, avoids duplicate version families, and serves only content-validated items (approved bank or auto-validated AI-source items) with confirmed concept tags. SQL items always come from the validated bank. With source AI, MCQ and essay items may be generated and must pass automated checks before entering the plan; Administrator approval is required only when a candidate is promoted into the validated bank; a single bank_mixed notice is shown when bank items fill part of an AI plan. An insufficient bank stops the start with an explicit shortage explanation instead of a reduced or relaxed session.

System lets new users register with email/password or Google/GitHub OAuth (verified email) and creates a Learner account only. Administrator accounts are provisioned only by existing administrators, start disabled, and all role changes are recorded in an immutable audit log. A Learner may request promotion to Administrator; an existing administrator with role-management capability reviews and grants or denies the request through the audited role-management workflow (no self-service promotion endpoint).
Web pages load within 1.5 seconds; API endpoints respond within 500 milliseconds for standard requests.
FastAPI asynchronous routes and optimized frontend bundles.
Learner SQL queries run inside a dedicated isolated container with a 3-second statement timeout and limited memory, preventing server overloads.

A dedicated Docker container running PostgreSQL with a read-only learner role that accepts SELECT statements only, enforced statement timeouts, disabled network access, and no access to production data.
Web platform maintains dependable uptime during scheduled learner practice sessions.
Containerized deployment with automatic health monitoring and restart policies.

Platform easily handles a full class section of 100 learners taking a practice session at the same time.
Stateless backend design with PostgreSQL connection pooling.

Learner names and identifying numbers are removed before any text is sent to external LLM Provider APIs for essay grading, mapping/tag suggestions, or gap explanations. Unpublished scores, provisional competency profiles and gap results are withheld from the learner until the administrator approves and publishes the session, and are visible only to authorized reviewers before that point.
Data sanitization gateway that strips personal details before external API requests; release-scoped read checks ensure only published results enter learner-facing profiles and analytics.
Clean, well-documented source code with automated unit tests for core backend services.
Automated unit test suite (pytest) executed before merges with clear documentation.

In the default bank source, AI-generated question candidates never block or fail a practice session; automated checks and Administrator approval precede bank entry. In the optional AI source, a failed generation falls back to bank items with a single bank_mixed notice instead of serving an unvalidated item.

Generate-ahead pipeline with PostgreSQL-backed checks, Administrator approval, a frozen validated practice plan, a validated item pool for BANK mode, and fail-closed AI delivery with an audited notice.

Learner SQL queries run inside a dedicated Docker sandbox container with memory capped at 256 MB and execution capped at 3 seconds via statement_timeout to prevent server overloads or runaway queries. The sandbox accepts read-only SELECT statements only; DML/DDL are assessed through MCQ and essay.

External language model API calls are managed using PostgreSQL-backed response caching, durable asynchronous grading jobs in the FastAPI backend, and a cost-effective model from the configured provider to avoid delays.
The web interface runs smoothly on standard modern browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) using standard HTML5/CSS without requiring custom browser plugins.

Google/GitHub sign-in and sign-up use signed state, Google PKCE, verified email and a single-use handoff. Login and Register always show both choices; an unconfigured provider offers email sign-in. Matching verified emails link one account without changing roles. Both email and OAuth issue rotating access/refresh sessions; provider tokens are never stored or exposed to the browser.

The external LLM Provider assists with essay scoring against administrator-configured rubrics and generates evidence-linked gap explanations; it does not determine final competency. Administrators configure essay rubrics and review every submission; the platform applies a 70% passing target per concept. DBCAS deterministically aggregates recorded answer evidence into concept scores and ranks below-benchmark concepts by shortfall; every submission requires administrator approval of SQL and essay scores before publication. Gap explanations cannot change scores or order.

System Testing, Quality Assurance & User Feedback
API temperature is set to a low value (temperature = 0.1) with fixed seeds across repeated calls.
Prevents random score variations and ensures identical learner answers receive consistent grades.
Language model output is constrained to a predefined JSON schema containing numeric scores, rubric levels, and cited text.
Enables reliable automated parsing by the FastAPI backend and prevents free-form text hallucinations.
Prompts include explicit rubric level definitions (Complete, Mostly Complete, Partial, Incomplete) with concrete grading examples.
Ensures the AI acts strictly as an objective rubric evaluator rather than an unconstrained chatbot.

Administrators configure essay rubrics and review every submission, apply the platform's 70% passing target, and approve AI-generated question candidates before bank entry. The LLM provides rubric-assisted essay scores and evidence-linked gap explanations. DBCAS applies fixed rules to recorded answer evidence to compute concept competency and rank gaps by shortfall; gap explanations do not change scores or order. Every submission requires administrator approval of SQL and essay scores before publication.
Keeps evaluation rules and validated question content under Administrator control, with defined system rules for scores and rankings and human sign-off where required.
Learners writing harmful SQL queries or infinite loops that could overload the server.

• Enforce a strict 3-second statement timeout and a 256 MB memory limit on the sandbox container. • Run queries in an isolated, unprivileged container under a read-only role and accept SELECT statements only; DML/DDL are assessed through MCQ and essay. • Roll back every learner transaction and reset the sandbox schema between assessment sessions.
Language model giving slightly different scores or inaccurate feedback on written essay answers.

• Use low temperature settings and require structured JSON output. • Grade using detailed rubrics that require citing specific sentences from learner answers. • Route every session through the administrator review queue and publish only after approval.
External LLM Provider fees or slow network responses during busy assessment sessions.
• Use a fast, cost-effective model from the chosen LLM provider. • Cache identical evaluation queries in a PostgreSQL table and process grading as durable asynchronous jobs.
Limited access to real university learner exam archives due to school privacy policies.

• Build a self-contained benchmark dataset of realistic, difficulty-tagged sample questions, schemas, and answers large enough to support personalized plan assembly. • Include common learner mistakes to test the evaluation pipeline thoroughly.
Sprint tasks running behind schedule, risking university review deadlines.
• Follow strict two-week sprints with velocity tracking at every retrospective.• Focus on completing core features first for a solid Midterm demonstration.
A personalized selection repeatedly over-samples narrow or poorly matched questions, producing an inaccurate ability estimate.

• Spread the plan across the selected concepts as far as the count allows: freeze the complete practice plan before serving and disclose any widening to related concepts or bands. • Log every selection decision and use validated fallback items so no session waits for AI generation.
